lesson.title: Three Views of the Same Amplifier: Voltage, Current, and Power Gain
lesson.summary: An amplifier's performance can be described by voltage gain, current gain, or power gain, and because power equals voltage times current, these three numbers are not independent but are tied together by a simple relationship.
lesson.body:
Depending on the application, an engineer may care about different aspects of what an amplifier does to a signal. An audio preamp is chosen mainly for its voltage gain, since the next stage responds to voltage. A speaker driver stage is chosen partly for its current gain, since driving a low impedance speaker coil requires substantial current. Power gain, covered in the previous chapter, is the combined effect of both, and it turns out to be their product.

Voltage gain is defined as Av = Vout / Vin, and current gain as Ai = Iout / Iin. Since power is the product of voltage and current (P = V times I), it follows algebraically that Ap = Pout / Pin = (Vout times Iout) / (Vin times Iin) = (Vout / Vin) times (Iout / Iin) = Av times Ai. Power gain is not a separate, independently arising quantity, it is simply what you get when voltage gain and current gain both act on the same signal at once.

Suppose an amplifier stage has an input voltage of 10 millivolts and produces an output voltage of 2 volts, giving a voltage gain of Av = 2 V / 0.01 V = 200. Suppose further that the input current is 1 milliamp and the output current is 50 milliamps, giving a current gain of Ai = 50 mA / 1 mA = 50. The power gain predicted by multiplying these is Ap = 200 times 50 = 10,000. We can check this directly from the definition of power gain: input power is Pin = Vin times Iin = 0.01 V times 0.001 A = 0.00001 W, or 10 microwatts, and output power is Pout = Vout times Iout = 2 V times 0.05 A = 0.1 W, or 100 milliwatts. Dividing gives Pout / Pin = 0.1 / 0.00001 = 10,000, exactly matching Av times Ai.

Because voltage gain and current gain are each proportional to a single quantity (not a product of two), while power gain scales as their product, voltage and current gain in decibels use a factor of 20 rather than 10, that is, Av(dB) = 20 log10(Av). This keeps the decibel value consistent regardless of whether you compute it from voltage, current, or power, since power is proportional to voltage squared (for a fixed resistance) and log(x squared) contributes an extra factor of 2.

Operational amplifiers, the subject of the rest of this unit, are almost always characterized by their voltage gain rather than current or power gain, because the internal design of the amplifier and the external resistor networks used to control it are most naturally described in terms of input and output voltages. The next chapter looks at just how enormous that voltage gain is inside a bare op-amp before any external control is applied.
